quizzes.title: Module 1, Week 1 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the relationship between anatomy and physiology?

answers.text: Anatomy and physiology are unrelated fields of biology.
Anatomy describes structure; physiology describes function — and the two cannot be fully understood apart from each other.
Anatomy is a subdiscipline of physiology that focuses on cells.
Anatomy describes function; physiology describes structure.

questions.text: The six levels of structural organization in the human body, from smallest to largest, are:

answers.text: Chemical, cellular, organ, tissue, organ system, organismal
Cellular, chemical, tissue, organ, organ system, organismal
Chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system, organismal
Chemical, tissue, cellular, organ, organ system, organismal

questions.text: Which body plane divides the body into anterior and posterior portions?
Homeostasis is best described as:

answers.text: The body's tendency to remain motionless when at rest.
The maintenance of stable internal conditions in the face of external change.
The growth of an organism over its lifespan.
The accumulation of waste products inside cells.

questions.text: Which of the following is not one of the four major classes of biological macromolecule?
Enzymes increase the rate of biochemical reactions by raising the activation energy required for the reaction.

questions.text: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium looks layered under a microscope because:

answers.text: It genuinely has multiple stacked layers of cells.
It is a single layer of cells whose varying heights and nucleus positions create the appearance of layers.
It is stratified squamous epithelium viewed at an angle.
It sheds and regenerates faster than other epithelium.

questions.text: A tendon connecting muscle to bone is best classified as:
The defining shared feature of muscle tissue and nervous tissue is:

answers.text: Both are excitable — they maintain a membrane voltage and can generate action potentials.

Which epidermal cell type is responsible for producing melanin?

quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Which of the following is not one of the five major functions of the skeletal system?

answers.text: Detection of pain stimuli at the skin

questions.text: Compact bone differs from spongy bone in that:

answers.text: Compact bone is non-living; spongy bone is alive.
Compact bone is dense and forms the outer shell and shaft of bones; spongy bone is porous and forms the interior, particularly at the ends of long bones.
Compact bone contains marrow; spongy bone does not.
Spongy bone is found only in children.

questions.text: Which bone cell type is responsible for breaking down bone matrix and releasing calcium into the bloodstream?
Which of the following is correctly paired?

Which of the following is true about the hyoid bone?

answers.text: It is part of the cervical spine.
It is the only bone in the body that does not form a joint with another bone.
It is the smallest bone in the inner ear.
It is found only in children and is absorbed during puberty.

questions.text: A normal adult vertebral column contains:

answers.text: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx
5 cervical, 12 thoracic, 7 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx
12 cervical, 7 thoracic, 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx
7 cervical, 7 thoracic, 12 lumbar vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx

questions.text: The atlas (C1) and the axis (C2) work together as a single articulating unit: rotation between them (around the dens of C2) is what allows you to turn your head from side to side to indicate "no."
A patient's X-ray shows a fracture at the styloid process of the temporal bone. This bony landmark is best described as:

answers.text: A rounded depression that a tendon rests inside
A thin, pointed projection that anchors muscles and ligaments of the tongue and neck
A large opening through which the spinal cord passes
The smooth, cup-shaped socket that receives the mandibular condyle

questions.text: Match each bone marking to its correct classification.

quizzes.title: Module 3, Week 2 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: The two regions of an intervertebral disc are:

answers.text: The annulus fibrosus and the nucleus pulposus

questions.text: The sacrum is unusual in that it:

answers.text: Began life as 5 separate vertebrae that fuse together by adulthood.
Is the only bone that articulates with the coccyx.

questions.text: Which group of ribs has its costal cartilages attached directly to the sternum?

answers.text: All 12 pairs attach directly to the sternum.

questions.text: The sternal angle is a useful clinical landmark because it aligns with the second pair of ribs and is used to count ribs.
The shoulder girdle bones include:
Which feature of the scapula directly articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint?
When you turn your forearm from palm-up to palm-down (pronation):

answers.text: The radius stays still and the ulna rotates around it.
The radius rotates around the ulna; the ulna stays roughly still.
Both bones rotate equally around the elbow joint.
Neither bone moves — only the wrist rotates.

questions.text: Match each region to its bone count for one upper limb.
A rib whose costal cartilage attaches not to the sternum but to the cartilage of rib 7 belongs to which category?
Match each bony landmark to the bone it belongs to.

quizzes.title: Module 3, Week 3 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Each os coxa is the fusion of three bones. Which set names all three correctly?
Compared with the glenoid cavity of the scapula, the acetabulum of the os coxa is:
The medial malleolus is:

answers.text: A bump on the inner side of the elbow.
The distal end of the tibia, forming the inner side of the ankle.
The distal end of the fibula, forming the outer side of the ankle.

questions.text: The patella is a sesamoid bone — a bone that develops inside the quadriceps tendon.
Which of the following is not one of the six features of a synovial joint?
Match each synovial joint type to a body example.
In osteoporosis, the imbalance is:

answers.text: Osteoblasts outpace osteoclasts, causing bones to thicken.
Osteoclasts outpace osteoblasts, causing bones to become porous and brittle.

questions.text: The four stages of bone fracture healing, in order, are:

answers.text: Bony callus → fibrocartilaginous callus → hematoma → remodeling
Hematoma → fibrocartilaginous callus → bony callus → remodeling
Remodeling → hematoma → bony callus → fibrocartilaginous callus
Fibrocartilaginous callus → hematoma → remodeling → bony callus

quizzes.title: Module 4, Week 1 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the three muscle types is correct?

answers.text: Smooth muscle is striated and voluntary.
Cardiac muscle is non-striated and voluntary.
Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary.
All three muscle types are involuntary.

questions.text: Intercalated discs are a defining feature of:
Match each muscle type to its primary location:

answers.right: Attached to the bones of the skeleton
Walls of the stomach and intestines, walls of blood vessels

questions.text: A muscle is wrapped, from outer to inner, in connective tissue sheaths called:
A sarcomere is best defined as:

answers.text: A single muscle fiber from end to end
The region between two Z-discs along a myofibril
The connective tissue sheath surrounding a muscle fiber
The structure that stores calcium inside a muscle fiber

questions.text: During the cross-bridge cycle, the role of ATP binding (as distinguished from ATP hydrolysis) is to:

answers.text: Cock the myosin head back to its high-energy position
Release the myosin head from actin so it can detach
Move the thin filament toward the M-line

questions.text: Calcium triggers contraction by:

answers.text: Binding directly to myosin heads and rotating them
Binding to troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the actin binding sites
Hydrolyzing ATP inside the myosin head
Breaking down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft

questions.text: During a sarcomere contraction, which of the following does not change in length?
The neurotransmitter released at the skeletal neuromuscular junction is acetylcholine, and the enzyme that breaks it down in the synaptic cleft is acetylcholinesterase.

quizzes.title: Module 4, Week 2 — Reading Quiz

questions.text: Which of the following is not an action of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM)?

answers.text: Unilateral contraction rotates the head to the opposite side
Unilateral contraction tilts the head toward the same shoulder

questions.text: Match each head/neck muscle to its primary action:

answers.text: Muscles that move the head on the neck

questions.text: The three columns of the erector spinae group, from lateral (out at the sides) to medial (close to the spine), are:
The latissimus dorsi inserts on:

answers.text: The medial border of the scapula
The intertubercular groove of the humerus, on the front of the upper arm

questions.text: Which statement about the diaphragm is correct?

answers.text: Contracting the diaphragm pushes the dome upward and shrinks the thoracic cavity.
Contracting the diaphragm flattens the dome and enlarges the thoracic cavity, drawing air into the lungs.
The diaphragm is smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle.
The diaphragm is innervated by the vagus nerve.

questions.text: Match each diaphragm opening to the structure that passes through it:

quizzes.title: Module 4, Week 3 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Which muscle is the primary hip flexor, working antagonistically to the gluteus maximus?
Which calf-region muscle crosses only the ankle, not the knee?
Which of the three ATP-producing systems can sustain muscle contraction for the shortest time?

answers.text: All three are sustained for about the same length of time

questions.text: Match each muscle fiber type to the activity it is best suited for:

When a muscle gets larger from heavy resistance training, the number of muscle fibers does not increase — each existing fiber becomes thicker by adding more myofibrils, with help from satellite cells that donate nuclei.
Match each condition to the point in the contraction chain where it fails:

answers.right: Antibodies destroy ACh receptors on the motor end plate
A toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmission in the spinal cord
The muscle fiber's membrane ruptures, releasing myoglobin

questions.text: Nerve agents such as sarin cause sustained muscle contraction (flexion paralysis) because they:

answers.text: Destroy ACh receptors on the motor end plate
Block voltage-gated calcium channels in the axon terminal
Permanently disable acetylcholinesterase, so ACh is never cleared from the synaptic cleft
Prevent the sarcoplasmic reticulum from releasing calcium

quizzes.title: Module 5, Week 1 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of:

answers.text: The brain and all cranial nerves.
The brain and the spinal cord.
The brain, the spinal cord, and the spinal nerves.

questions.text: Which division of the peripheral nervous system carries the conscious command to contract a skeletal muscle?
Match each neuron part to its function.

answers.right: Contains the nucleus and most organelles
Carries the signal away from the cell body
Forms synapses with the next cell

questions.text: Which glial cell is responsible for producing the myelin sheath in the central nervous system?
The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is approximately:
During the depolarization phase of an action potential, which ion moves and in which direction?

answers.text: Na⁺ moves out of the cell

questions.text: An action potential is "all-or-nothing" — once threshold is reached, the spike fires at full size regardless of how strong the original stimulus was.
In a chemical synapse, what triggers the release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic terminal?

answers.text: Sodium rushing out of the terminal

questions.text: A reflex arc has five components. Which of the following lists them in correct order from stimulus to response?

answers.text: Sensory neuron → sensory receptor → integration center → effector → motor neuron
Sensory receptor → motor neuron → integration center → sensory neuron → effector
Sensory receptor → sensory neuron → integration center → motor neuron → effector
Effector → motor neuron → integration center → sensory neuron → sensory receptor

questions.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is caused by damage to which glial cell type, and the myelin it produces?

quizzes.title: Module 5, Week 2 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: The four major divisions of the brain are the brainstem, cerebellum, diencephalon, and cerebrum. Which one is responsible for the moment-to-moment fine-tuning of voluntary movement and balance?
Damage to which part of the brain is most likely to be immediately fatal because it stops breathing?
Match each cerebral lobe to one of its primary functions.

answers.right: Primary motor cortex; planning; speech production (Broca's area)

questions.text: The three meningeal layers, from outermost to innermost, are:

answers.text: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater

questions.text: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is produced by the choroid plexus and flows through the four ventricles of the brain, helping to cushion the CNS against mechanical shock.
In a cross-section of the spinal cord, the cell bodies of motor neurons that send axons to skeletal muscle are located in the:

answers.text: Dorsal (posterior) horn of the gray matter
Ventral (anterior) horn of the gray matter

questions.text: A high cervical spinal cord injury (C1–C3) is often immediately life-threatening because it can paralyze:

answers.text: The diaphragm (since the phrenic nerve emerges from C3–C5)
The heart (since cardiac nerves emerge from C1–C2)

questions.text: How many pairs of cranial nerves and how many pairs of spinal nerves does the human body have?
Clinical application. Which brain division would most likely be damaged in a patient showing dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting a target when reaching for it)?

quizzes.title: Module 5, Week 3 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Which division of the autonomic nervous system is most active during "fight or flight"?
The vagus nerve (CN X) carries the majority of which kind of autonomic outflow?

answers.text: Parasympathetic to abdominal and thoracic organs

questions.text: Match each eye structure to its function.

answers.right: Transparent dome at the front of the eye that does most of the light bending
Adjustable focusing element controlled by the ciliary body

questions.text: Rods and cones differ in which of the following ways?

answers.text: Rods detect color; cones detect light intensity only.
Cones are most concentrated at the fovea; rods are more numerous overall.
Cones work better in dim light; rods are responsible for sharp daylight vision.
Rods are responsible for fine spatial detail; cones are not.

questions.text: The three auditory ossicles, in the order a sound wave passes through them, are:
Which structure in the inner ear is primarily responsible for hearing (as opposed to balance)?
Olfaction (smell) is unusual among the senses because its signals reach cortical and limbic regions of the brain without being relayed through the thalamus first.
A signal from a fingertip mechanoreceptor reaches the cerebral cortex by way of:

answers.text: Spinal nerve → dorsal column → medulla (crossing) → thalamus → parietal lobe (somatosensory cortex)
Cranial nerve VIII → cochlear nuclei → temporal lobe

questions.text: A patient presents with sudden one-sided facial drooping and cannot fully close one eye. Which cranial nerve is most likely injured?

quizzes.title: Module 6, Week 1 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes an endocrine gland from an exocrine gland?

answers.text: Endocrine glands secrete their products through ducts; exocrine glands do not.
Endocrine glands secrete their products directly into the bloodstream; exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface.
Endocrine glands act locally; exocrine glands act systemically.
Endocrine glands are made of muscle tissue; exocrine glands are made of epithelial tissue.

questions.text: A hormone classified as a steroid is most likely to:

answers.text: Bind a receptor on the surface of the target cell and trigger a cAMP cascade within seconds.
Bind a receptor inside the target cell, change gene expression, and produce effects that last for hours to days.
Be water-soluble and unable to cross cell membranes.
Be made of a long chain of amino acids.

questions.text: The pancreas is both an endocrine and an exocrine organ.
Which of these tasks is best handled by the endocrine system rather than the nervous system?

answers.text: Pulling your hand away from a hot stove
Blinking in response to a bright flash
Coordinating the body's growth spurt across many tissues over months

questions.text: Match each anterior pituitary hormone to its target.
ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are released from the posterior pituitary. Where are they actually made?
A patient has a low blood T₄ level. If the disease is in the thyroid gland itself (primary hypothyroidism), what will TSH look like?

answers.text: High — the pituitary is trying to compensate by driving the broken thyroid harder.
Low — the pituitary has shut down along with the thyroid.
Normal — TSH does not respond to thyroid disease.
Undetectable — TSH is only released when T₄ is high.

questions.text: When blood calcium falls below normal, parathyroid hormone (PTH) acts on three organs to raise it. Which of the following is not one of PTH's three target organs?

answers.text: Small intestine (indirectly, via active vitamin D)

quizzes.title: Module 6, Week 2 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: The three zones of the adrenal cortex, from outermost to innermost, are:

answers.text: Zona reticularis → zona fasciculata → zona glomerulosa
Zona fasciculata → zona reticularis → zona glomerulosa
Zona glomerulosa → zona fasciculata → zona reticularis
Zona medullaris → zona glomerulosa → zona fasciculata

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the adrenal medulla?

answers.text: An endocrine gland controlled by ACTH from the anterior pituitary.
A modified sympathetic ganglion whose cells release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood.
A region of the kidney that produces aldosterone.
The hormone-producing region of the parathyroid.

questions.text: Match each adrenal hormone to its main action.

answers.right: Retains sodium and water in the kidney
Fast fight-or-flight effects across the body
Weak androgen; contributes to puberty changes and (in women) most circulating androgen

questions.text: Which cells of the pancreas produce insulin?

answers.text: Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans
Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans
Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas
Delta cells of the islets of Langerhans

questions.text: Glucagon raises blood glucose mainly by acting on the liver, where it triggers glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
Which of the following best distinguishes type 1 from type 2 diabetes mellitus?

answers.text: Type 1 is caused by tissue resistance to insulin; type 2 is caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells.
Type 1 is caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells (so there is little or no insulin); type 2 involves insulin resistance with eventual beta-cell exhaustion.
Type 1 only occurs in adults; type 2 only occurs in children.
Type 1 is treated with diet alone; type 2 always requires insulin injections.

questions.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released by which organ, and what does it do?

answers.text: Kidney — promotes red blood cell production
Heart (atria) — tells the kidney to dump sodium, lowering blood volume and pressure
Adrenal cortex — raises blood pressure by retaining salt

questions.text: A patient develops Cushing's syndrome from chronic use of an oral steroid medication. Which of the following hormone patterns is most likely on a blood test?

answers.text: High cortisol; high ACTH (both elevated together)
High cortisol (from the medication); low ACTH (suppressed by negative feedback)

quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: By volume, an adult's blood is approximately:

Red blood cells contain a nucleus but no mitochondria.
A single hemoglobin molecule contains four subunits, each cradling a heme group with one iron atom. How many O₂ molecules can a single hemoglobin molecule carry at maximum saturation?

answers.right: Round, with a single huge nucleus and very little cytoplasm

questions.text: Platelets are best described as:

answers.text: Small whole cells with their own nuclei

A type of leukocyte specialized for clotting

questions.text: During coagulation, the enzyme thrombin converts:
A Type O-negative donor can give red cells safely to:

answers.text: Type O recipients only, regardless of Rh
Any ABO/Rh recipient — O-negative is the universal red-cell donor

quizzes.title: Module 7, Week 2 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

questions.text: The pericardial fluid is found between which two layers?

answers.text: Fibrous pericardium and the parietal serous pericardium
Parietal serous pericardium and visceral serous pericardium (epicardium)
Visceral serous pericardium and the myocardium

questions.text: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood AND is classified as an artery?
The left ventricular myocardium is dramatically thicker than the right ventricular myocardium primarily because:

answers.text: The left ventricle holds more blood per stroke
The left ventricle must generate enough pressure to push blood through the high-resistance systemic circuit
The left ventricle contains the conduction system
The left ventricle pumps faster than the right

questions.text: Match each valve to its location and number of cusps.

answers.right: Between right atrium and right ventricle; 3 cusps
At base of pulmonary trunk; 3 pocket cusps
Between left atrium and left ventricle; 2 cusps
At base of aorta; 3 pocket cusps

questions.text: The chordae tendineae anchor the cusps of the semilunar (pulmonary and aortic) valves.
The correct order of the cardiac conduction pathway is:

answers.text: SA node → bundle of His → AV node → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
AV node → SA node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
SA node → AV node → Purkinje fibers → bundle of His → bundle branches

questions.text: The S1 ("lub") heart sound is produced by:

answers.text: Closure of the AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) at the start of ventricular systole
Closure of the semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) at the start of diastole

questions.text: A patient with a complete occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery would primarily lose blood supply to:

answers.text: The right atrium and SA node
The right ventricle and posterior wall of the left ventricle
The anterior wall of the left ventricle, the apex, and the anterior interventricular septum

questions.text: The coronary arteries fill primarily during ventricular diastole, not systole.

quizzes.title: Module 7, Week 3 — Reading Quiz
quizzes.description: Auto-graded reading quiz for this week. One attempt; answer order is shuffled.

Right subclavian, brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid

questions.text: The radial pulse you feel at the wrist is generated by:

answers.text: The radial artery (a terminal branch of the brachial artery)

questions.text: Match each abdominal aorta branch to what it primarily supplies.

answers.right: First half of large intestine + small intestine

questions.text: The skeletal-muscle pump that helps return venous blood from the legs depends on:

The pulmonary veins → the left atrium → the systemic circulation

questions.text: Resistance to blood flow is most strongly affected by:

answers.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy, increased stroke risk, and chronic kidney disease
Reduced cardiac output independent of vessel disease

questions.text: Match each fetal shunt or vessel to what it bypasses or carries.

answers.right: Right atrium → left atrium, bypassing the lungs
Pulmonary trunk → aorta, bypassing the lungs
Carries oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus

Match each condition to the point in the contraction chain where it fails:

A toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmission in the spinal cord
The muscle fiber's membrane ruptures, releasing myoglobin

questions.text: Which division of the peripheral nervous system carries the conscious command to contract a skeletal muscle?
The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is approximately:
In a chemical synapse, what triggers the release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic terminal?

answers.text: Sodium rushing out of the terminal

questions.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is caused by damage to which glial cell type, and the myelin it produces?
Match each cerebral lobe to one of its primary functions.

answers.right: Primary motor cortex; planning; speech production (Broca's area)

questions.text: In a cross-section of the spinal cord, the cell bodies of motor neurons that send axons to skeletal muscle are located in the:

answers.text: Dorsal (posterior) horn of the gray matter
Ventral (anterior) horn of the gray matter

questions.text: Clinical application. Which brain division would most likely be damaged in a patient showing dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting a target when reaching for it)?
Match each eye structure to its function.

answers.right: Transparent dome at the front of the eye that does most of the light bending
Adjustable focusing element controlled by the ciliary body

questions.text: The three auditory ossicles, in the order a sound wave passes through them, are:
A signal from a fingertip mechanoreceptor reaches the cerebral cortex by way of:

answers.text: Spinal nerve → dorsal column → medulla (crossing) → thalamus → parietal lobe (somatosensory cortex)
Cranial nerve VIII → cochlear nuclei → temporal lobe

questions.text: A hormone classified as a steroid is most likely to:

answers.text: Bind a receptor on the surface of the target cell and trigger a cAMP cascade within seconds.
Bind a receptor inside the target cell, change gene expression, and produce effects that last for hours to days.
Be water-soluble and unable to cross cell membranes.
Be made of a long chain of amino acids.

questions.text: Match each anterior pituitary hormone to its target.
A patient has a low blood T₄ level. If the disease is in the thyroid gland itself (primary hypothyroidism), what will TSH look like?

answers.text: High — the pituitary is trying to compensate by driving the broken thyroid harder.
Low — the pituitary has shut down along with the thyroid.
Normal — TSH does not respond to thyroid disease.
Undetectable — TSH is only released when T₄ is high.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the adrenal medulla?

answers.text: An endocrine gland controlled by ACTH from the anterior pituitary.
A modified sympathetic ganglion whose cells release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood.
A region of the kidney that produces aldosterone.
The hormone-producing region of the parathyroid.

questions.text: Glucagon raises blood glucose mainly by acting on the liver, where it triggers glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released by which organ, and what does it do?

answers.text: Kidney — promotes red blood cell production
Heart (atria) — tells the kidney to dump sodium, lowering blood volume and pressure
Adrenal cortex — raises blood pressure by retaining salt

questions.text: Which plasma protein is most responsible for maintaining the osmotic pull that keeps water inside the bloodstream?
Which of the following is the most abundant white blood cell in normal circulating blood, and what is its primary job?
During coagulation, the enzyme thrombin converts:
Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood AND is classified as an artery?
The chordae tendineae anchor the cusps of the semilunar (pulmonary and aortic) valves.
The S1 ("lub") heart sound is produced by:

answers.text: Closure of the AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) at the start of ventricular systole
Closure of the semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) at the start of diastole

questions.text: Which three branches arise from the aortic arch, in order from right to left as they leave it?

answers.text: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian
Left subclavian, left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk
Right subclavian, brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid
Brachiocephalic trunk, right subclavian, left common carotid

questions.text: The skeletal-muscle pump that helps return venous blood from the legs depends on:

answers.text: Smooth muscle in the vein wall contracting on its own
Surrounding muscle contraction squeezing the veins, with one-way valves preventing backflow
Gravity pulling blood toward the heart

questions.text: A patient with chronic, untreated hypertension is most likely to develop, over years:

answers.text: Left ventricular hypertrophy, increased stroke risk, and chronic kidney disease
Reduced cardiac output independent of vessel disease
